To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the liver clears gastrin and cholecytostokinin peptides, and the degree of hepatic clearance depends upon the length of the peptide.
gastrin and CCK peptides longer than seven or eight amino acids traverse the rat liver intact.
the liver is a barrier to the systemic delivery of gastrin peptides shorter than 8 residues in length, and that the liver is an effective clearance mechanism for CCK tetrapeptides.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the liver in the metabolism of gastrin and other peptides.
the regulation of gastric acid secretion.
the role of the gastrointestinal tract in the pathogenesis of the liver diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the liver is not a major site of gastrin degradation.
the liver is an important site for inactivation of gastrin peptides and that it may also play an important role in inactivation of cholecystokinins.
the liver is a major organ in the clearance of gastrin, and to a lesser extent, cholecystokin peptides.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the liver does not appear to be an important site of gastrin and CCK degradation.
the liver is a barrier to gastrin and CCK peptides less than 7 amino acids in length.
the liver is not a barrier to the systemic circulation of biologically active gastrin and cholecytokinin peptides, however, small fragments are inactivated by liver metabolism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver is a major organ for inactivation of gastrin peptides.
the liver does a good job of removing small peptides from the blood stream.
the liver can clear small fragments of gastrin or cholecystokinn, but it can’t do that for longer chains of these hormones.
